q: It is 16:30 at the base in Lefkas. The technician hands you the form and says he will start with the engine. How do you run the walk-round?
a: Outside first from the quay, bow to stern on both sides, then the deck, then the rig
o: Engine and inside first, the hull from the quay once he has left
Deck and rig first while it is light, the hull from the dinghy tomorrow
Whatever order he prefers, as long as the engine runs before you sign
why: A fixed order — hull both sides, deck, rig — is how nothing gets missed; the hull is the deposit.

fig.title: Check-in, Lefkas
lines: Technician: 'Engine first, then inside'
Form: boat outline and a remarks box
Three more boats waiting for him

q: At 17:10 the technician says this and heads for the next boat. What do you do?
a: Ask him to stay for the walk-round — what you find alone is disputed on Friday
o: Walk round alone and list everything; the office will accept the list
Sign the hull section now and photograph the boat after he leaves
Agree; a photographed walk-round is as good as a witnessed one
why: Damage goes on the form with the base's technician present and initialling; notes made alone are your word against theirs.

fig.title: Technician
lines: 'Walk round yourself, I have three more'
'Bring the form to the office by 18:00'
Form still blank for hull and deck

q: On the port bow, 40 cm aft of the stem, you find this. It is not on the form. What do you do?
a: Photograph it with a coin for scale, write 'chip 3 cm, star cracks' on the outline, have him initial
o: Write 'scratches, port bow' in the remarks box and move on to the deck
Leave it — chips under 5 cm are normal wear and are never charged
Ask the base to fill and polish it before you leave the dock
why: Size, place and a photo with scale; star cracks mean impact, so write cracks, not scratches.

fig.title: Port bow: gelcoat chip 3 cm
lines: Star cracks round the chip
Below the toe rail, 40 cm aft of the stem
Form: nothing marked at the bow

q: From the quay you look along the port side at the waterline. What goes on the form?
a: 'Weed on waterline' and 'old repair, stbd quarter' with a photo — neither is yours
o: A request for a diver before you sign — fouling slows the boat and heats the engine
'Crack, starboard quarter' — so the repair cannot be charged to you later
Nothing — the waterline and old repairs are not deposit items
why: Fouling and old repairs are the base's; writing them down with a photo is what keeps them the base's.

fig.title: Waterline, from the quay
lines: Green weed along the waterline
Stern 5 cm low: tanks full, 6 bags aboard
Stbd quarter: brighter gelcoat patch, sound

q: Moored stern-to in Alimos, the water is clear enough to see the keel. What do you do before you go aboard?
a: Photograph both, write them on the form, and watch the rudder while he turns the wheel lock to lock
o: Note the rudder only; the keel is below the waterline and is not on the form
Ask for a haul-out before you accept the boat — a scuffed keel means a grounding
Note nothing; the technician has seen the keel and says it is only sand
why: A keel scuff at check-in that is not on the form becomes your grounding at check-out.

fig.title: Stern, from the quay
lines: Rudder: trailing edge chipped, 5 cm
Keel leading edge: scuffed, paint gone
Technician: 'a bit of sand, nothing'

q: You check the bathing platform before the crew arrives with the bags. What do you ask for?
a: The rung and the shower head fixed before you leave; the hinge play on the form with a photo
o: Nothing fixed — write all three on the form and manage with a bucket
The hinge rebuilt before you leave; the rung and the shower are wear
A tape repair on the rung yourself; note the hinge and the shower
why: A cracked rung breaks under a wet crew member; the rest is noted so it is not charged on Friday.

fig.title: Bathing platform
lines: Ladder: lowers; top rung cracked
Platform hinge: 1 cm play, lifts with a clunk
Deck shower: head missing

q: You lean on the starboard guardrail by the gate and find this. What do you do?
a: Ask the base to fix all three before you leave — the guardrail is what keeps the crew aboard
o: Write all three on the form and seize the hook with a lanyard
Tighten the stanchion yourself; the wire and the hook are cosmetic
Tell the crew to use the port side and note it on the form
why: A loose stanchion or a frayed lifeline fails when someone falls on it; the base fixes it, not the form.

q: In the forecabin you look at the hatch and the portlight. What do you do?
a: Photograph the crack and ask for the lens taped and the seal replaced — a wave fills that bunk
o: Note the crack; keep the hatch shut all week and the bunk stays dry
Ask for the portlight handle freed; the hatch is noted as wear
Note all three and ask for a tarpaulin for the foredeck
why: A hatch that does not seal takes green water on the foredeck; a cracked lens is a deposit item unless noted.

fig.title: Forecabin hatch
lines: Lens: 8 cm crack from the hinge corner
Seal perished; hatch does not dog down tight
Port portlight: closes, handle stiff

q: Walking the port side deck you press with your heel by the chainplates. What goes on the form?
a: All three with photos; the soft spot and the raised bolts the technician initials
o: The soft spot only — worn non-slip and proud bolts are wear
Nothing — deck wear is never a deposit item
A request for the deck re-cored before you sail
why: A soft spot is structural and may be blamed on your week; written and initialled now it stays the base's.

fig.title: Side deck, port
lines: Non-slip worn smooth by the shrouds
Soft spot 20 × 20 cm by the chainplate
Genoa track: two bolts standing proud

q: You open the cockpit lockers against the inventory. What do you do?
a: Count against the list; ask for a padlock, a latch that holds and the drain cleared
o: Sign the inventory — the count is the base's job, the latch you tie down
Note 'lockers OK'; a lid that does not latch is tied with a line
Ask for everything moved to the saloon so you can count it
why: An unlatched locker lid opens at sea and floods the lazarette; a blocked drain floods the cockpit.

fig.title: Cockpit lockers
lines: Port: fenders ×6, lines ×4, bucket
Lazarette: padlock missing, lid does not latch
Starboard drain holds water

q: At the binnacle you turn the wheel and work the lever with the engine off. What do you ask for?
a: The steering cables and the throttle cable adjusted now; the lock on the form
o: Nothing adjusted — note all three, charter wheels are always loose
The wheel lock replaced before you leave; play is normal, the lever you learn
A spray of lubricant on the lever yourself; note the play and the lock
why: Play in the steering is a loose cable or chain; a stiff throttle costs the moment you need astern in a berth.

fig.title: Binnacle
lines: Wheel: a quarter turn of play before the rudder moves
Wheel lock: slips under hand pressure
Throttle: stiff, two hands into astern

q: You check the canvas before the afternoon sun goes. What do you ask for?
a: The zip, strap and tear fixed before you leave; the window and the frame on the form with photos
o: Nothing fixed — canvas is wear, write all five items on the form
A new bimini fitted before you leave the dock, the sprayhood noted
The tear only; the zip, strap and frame are how the boat came
why: A tear grows in the first blow and a missing strap lets the bimini fold; what cannot be fixed now goes on the form.

fig.title: Sprayhood & bimini
lines: Sprayhood window scratched; port zip open at the foot
Bimini frame bent; one strap missing
Bimini: 15 cm tear at the aft seam

q: You check the standing rigging at deck level on both sides. What do you do?
a: A broken strand means the base's rigger before you sail; the split pin and tape are fitted now
o: Note both; tape the strand and ask for a split pin at your first port
Fit a pin yourself; one broken wire of nineteen is fine for a week
Ask for the rig tuned and tensioned before you accept the boat
why: A broken strand at the swage is the start of a failure; a turnbuckle without a split pin unwinds.

fig.title: Standing rigging, from deck
lines: Port cap shroud: turnbuckle split pin missing, no tape
Starboard lower: one broken strand at the swage
Chainplates: dry, no rust streaks

q: You stand at the mast foot on deck. What do you check by eye?
a: Up the groove: a straight mast, spreaders level with boots on; the collar sealed, the deck flat round the foot
o: Count the halyards and read the makers' label at the gooseneck
Push the mast at the gooseneck to feel for play in the step
The wind vane turning; the rest needs a bosun's chair
why: A bend, a drooping spreader or a dished deck round the foot are seen from the deck; the base's rigger does the rest.

q: You swing the boom and look at what holds it up. What do you ask the base for?
a: The gooseneck pin looked at now and a long line to rig a preventer; the rigid kicker needs no topping lift
o: A topping lift rigged to the masthead; the gooseneck play is normal and a sheet makes the preventer
Nothing — all three are how the boat was built and how it sailed last week
A new gooseneck fitting; the preventer is for ocean passages, not the Ionian
why: A rigid kicker carries the boom; a worn gooseneck pin and no preventer are what hurt crew in a gybe.

fig.title: Boom
lines: Gooseneck pin: worn, boom knocks when swung
Rigid kicker holds the boom; no topping lift
Preventer: no line aboard, no pad-eye forward

q: At the cabin-top winches you run each halyard and clutch. What do you do before you sign?
a: The clutch freed and the third handle found now; the chafe and the jaws on the form
o: Sign — a jammed clutch is opened at sea with a winch, two handles are plenty
Ask for the halyard replaced and a new self-tailer; the handle you buy
Note all four on the form and free the clutch with pliers once out
why: A clutch that will not release is a halyard you cannot drop; a missing handle is a deposit charge on Friday.

fig.note: Clutch #2 jammed shut · 2 of 3 winch handles found

q: At the bow you work the roller, the stopper and the cleat by hand. What do you do?
a: Ask for all three fixed before you leave — the cleat and the stopper take the mooring and anchor loads
o: Note all three; the windlass holds the chain and the starboard cleat does for mooring
Ask for the roller only; a loose cleat and a stopper are the base's wear
Tighten the cleat from below yourself and note the roller and the stopper
why: The chain stopper, not the windlass, holds the anchor load; a loose cleat is a line gone in a Meltemi night.

fig.title: Bow fitting
lines: Bow roller: pin bent, roller does not turn
Chain stopper: pawl missing
Port bow cleat: moves under hand pressure

q: The technician says the masthead was checked at the start of the season. How do you check it yourself before you sign?
a: Through binoculars from the quay: wind vane and cups turning, VHF antenna upright, light lenses whole
o: Send a crew member up in the bosun's chair with the technician on the winch
Switch the instruments on — a wind reading means the masthead is fine
You cannot from the deck; write 'masthead not inspected' on the form
why: Binoculars show a missing cup, a leaning antenna or a cracked lens from the quay; the season's start was months ago.

q: You find the pulpit bent to port. The technician says this. What do you do?
a: Write 'pulpit bent, port' on the outline now, photograph it and have him initial
o: Take his word — he knows the boat and the office has last week's form
Write it in the remarks box as 'general wear' to match the office
Ask the office for last week's check-out form before you continue
why: What counts on Friday is this form; 'general wear' and the technician's memory are not entries.

fig.title: Pulpit bent to port
lines: Technician: 'That's old, it's on the form already'
Form, boat outline: nothing at the bow
Remarks box: 'general wear'

q: In the catamaran saloon you find this, and the manager wants the form signed before the briefing. What do you do?
a: Do not sign until the entry reads 'crack 25 cm' with your photo — 'scratched' is your crack on Friday
o: Sign with 'see photo' beside the entry; the photo is dated and the office has a copy
Sign; a correction on Monday is in writing and better than an argument now
Sign and e-mail the office the photo tonight so the record is complete
why: You sign for the boat as the form describes it; a crack recorded as a scratch is charged to the deposit.

fig.title: Saloon forward window
lines: Crack 25 cm from the lower corner
Form: 'window scratched'
Manager: 'sign now, we correct it Monday'
